\section[fe]{\ur{ف} (fe) — the letter inside \ur{حافظ}}

\label{lesson:UR-W37-fe}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: write \ur{ھ} and \ur{گ} once each, and name them.

Now say \textbf{\ur{حافظ}} (\emph{hāfiz}), \textquotedblleft{}guardian\textquotedblright{}. You have read it for a long time. This lesson takes one letter out of it and puts it in your hand.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ur{ف}}
\textbf{\ur{ف}} — \emph{fe}, the sound \emph{f}.

It is inside \textbf{\ur{حافظ}} (\emph{hāfiz}). A small round \textbf{head} on a shallow tail, with \textbf{one dot above}.

\subsection*{Writing: \ur{ف}}
\hlblockfigure{\detokenize{figures/UR-W37-fe-filmstrip.pdf}}{How \ur{ف} is written, stroke by stroke}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start here: loop clockwise around the rounded head above the main line
  \item \textbf{2.} continue left through the shallow curved tail without lifting
  \item \textbf{3.} lift once, then place the upper dot last — and only now lift
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 1.}

\begin{quote}
Stroke order is one attested teaching order; hands and teachers vary. Source: Zer o Zabar, Fe, qāf, ṭe, ḍāl, and ṛe, independent \ur{ف} calligraphic and handwriting animations and Fe instructions (Northwestern University Libraries Open Textbook, 2026).
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\ur{حافظ}} and point at \ur{ف} inside it
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ur{ف} three times, saying \emph{f} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{گ}, then \ur{ف}, from memory
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ur{حافظ}} aloud once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which letter is this — \ur{ف}? (\textbf{fe}, \emph{f}.) Which word did it come from? (\textbf{\ur{حافظ}}, \emph{hāfiz}, \textquotedblleft{}guardian\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[qāf]{\ur{ق} (qāf) — the letter that opens \ur{قمیض}}

\label{lesson:UR-W37-qaf}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: write \ur{گ} and \ur{ف} once each, and name them.

Now say \textbf{\ur{قمیض}} (\emph{qamīz}), \textquotedblleft{}shirt\textquotedblright{}. You have read it for a long time. This lesson takes one letter out of it and puts it in your hand.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ur{ق}}
\textbf{\ur{ق}} — \emph{qāf}, a \emph{k} made far back in the throat.

It opens \textbf{\ur{قمیض}} (\emph{qamīz}), \textquotedblleft{}shirt\textquotedblright{}. Its head is the head of \textbf{\ur{ف}}, from the last lesson, but it carries \textbf{two dots}, and its bowl dips below the line.

\subsection*{Writing: \ur{ق}}
\hlblockfigure{\detokenize{figures/UR-W37-qaf-filmstrip.pdf}}{How \ur{ق} is written, stroke by stroke}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start here: loop clockwise around the rounded head above the main line
  \item \textbf{2.} continue down and left through the deep bowl without lifting
  \item \textbf{3.} after one lift, place the upper-right dot
  \item \textbf{4.} after another lift, place the upper-left dot — and only now lift
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 2.}

\begin{quote}
Stroke order is one attested teaching order; hands and teachers vary. Source: Zer o Zabar, Fe, qāf, ṭe, ḍāl, and ṛe, independent \ur{ق} calligraphic and handwriting animations and Qāf instructions (Northwestern University Libraries Open Textbook, 2026).
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\ur{قمیض}} and point at \ur{ق} inside it
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ur{ق} three times, saying \emph{q} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{ف}, then \ur{ق}, from memory
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ur{قمیض}} aloud once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which letter is this — \ur{ق}? (\textbf{qāf}, \emph{q}.) Which word did it come from? (\textbf{\ur{قمیض}}, \emph{qamīz}, \textquotedblleft{}shirt\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[zuād]{\ur{ض} (zuād) — the letter that ends \ur{قمیض}}

\label{lesson:UR-W37-zuad}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: write \ur{ف} and \ur{ق} once each, and name them.

Now say \textbf{\ur{قمیض}} (\emph{qamīz}), \textquotedblleft{}shirt\textquotedblright{}. You have read it for a long time. This lesson takes one letter out of it and puts it in your hand.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ur{ض}}
\textbf{\ur{ض}} — \emph{zuād}, the sound \emph{z}.

It ends \textbf{\ur{قمیض}} (\emph{qamīz}). An oval with a short tooth, a bowl, and \textbf{one dot above}. Urdu writes \emph{z} with more than one letter; \textbf{\ur{ض}} is the one that came with Arabic words like this.

\subsection*{Writing: \ur{ض}}
\hlblockfigure{\detokenize{figures/UR-W37-zuad-filmstrip.pdf}}{How \ur{ض} is written, stroke by stroke}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start here: close the elongated upper oval clockwise and finish its short tooth
  \item \textbf{2.} after one lift, restart below the oval and sweep through the lower bowl from right to left
  \item \textbf{3.} after another lift, place the dot above last — and only now lift
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 2.}

\begin{quote}
Stroke order is one attested teaching order; hands and teachers vary. Source: Zer o Zabar, Khe, ze, zal, swad, and zwad, independent \ur{ض} calligraphic and handwriting animations and Zwad instructions (Northwestern University Libraries Open Textbook, 2026).
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\ur{قمیض}} and point at \ur{ض} inside it
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ur{ض} three times, saying \emph{z} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{ق}, then \ur{ض}, from memory
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ur{قمیض}} aloud once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which letter is this — \ur{ض}? (\textbf{zuād}, \emph{z}.) Which word did it come from? (\textbf{\ur{قمیض}}, \emph{qamīz}, \textquotedblleft{}shirt\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[zoe]{\ur{ظ} (zoe) — the letter that ends \ur{حافظ}}

\label{lesson:UR-W37-zoe}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: write \ur{ق} and \ur{ض} once each, and name them.

Now say \textbf{\ur{حافظ}} (\emph{hāfiz}), \textquotedblleft{}guardian\textquotedblright{}. You have read it for a long time. This lesson takes one letter out of it and puts it in your hand.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ur{ظ}}
\textbf{\ur{ظ}} — \emph{zoe}, the sound \emph{z} again.

It ends \textbf{\ur{حافظ}} (\emph{hāfiz}). A closed \textbf{oval} on the line, a \textbf{tall upright}, and \textbf{one dot}. It sounds exactly like \textbf{\ur{ض}} from the last lesson: two spellings, one sound, both kept from the Arabic words they came with.

\subsection*{Writing: \ur{ظ}}
\hlblockfigure{\detokenize{figures/UR-W37-zoe-filmstrip.pdf}}{How \ur{ظ} is written, stroke by stroke}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start here: loop counterclockwise around the closed oval
  \item \textbf{2.} finish left along the baseline without lifting
  \item \textbf{3.} after one lift, draw the tall upright
  \item \textbf{4.} after another lift, place the single dot above — and only now lift
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 2.}

\begin{quote}
Stroke order is one attested teaching order; hands and teachers vary. Source: Zer o Zabar, To’e, zo’e, se, zhe, and ġhain, independent \ur{ظ} handwriting animation and Zo’e instructions (Northwestern University Libraries Open Textbook, 2026).
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\ur{حافظ}} and point at \ur{ظ} inside it
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ur{ظ} three times, saying \emph{z} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{ض}, then \ur{ظ}, from memory
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ur{حافظ}} aloud once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which letter is this — \ur{ظ}? (\textbf{zoe}, \emph{z}.) Which word did it come from? (\textbf{\ur{حافظ}}, \emph{hāfiz}, \textquotedblleft{}guardian\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[hamza]{\ur{ئ} (hamza) — the hamza on its seat in \ur{ہوئی}}

\label{lesson:UR-W37-hamza-seat}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: write \ur{ض} and \ur{ظ} once each, and name them.

Now say \textbf{\ur{ہوئی}} (\emph{huī}), \textquotedblleft{}happened (in pleased to meet you)\textquotedblright{}. You have read it for a long time. This lesson takes one letter out of it and puts it in your hand.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ur{ئ}}
\textbf{\ur{ئ}} — \emph{hamza} on its seat.

It is inside \textbf{\ur{ہوئی}} (\emph{huī}), the last word of \textbf{\ur{آپ} \ur{سے} \ur{مل} \ur{کر} \ur{خوشی} \ur{ہوئی}}. Say \emph{hu-ī}: two vowels side by side. The small \textbf{hamza} sits on a short tooth, its \textbf{seat}, and marks the place where one vowel ends and the next begins.

\subsection*{Writing: \ur{ئ}}
Put your pen on \ur{ئ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start this letter or which way to travel}. It is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\ur{ہوئی}} and point at \ur{ئ} inside it
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \ur{ئ} three times, saying \emph{hu-ī} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{ظ}, then \ur{ئ}, from memory
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ur{ہوئی}} aloud once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which letter is this — \ur{ئ}? (\textbf{hamza}, \emph{hu-ī}.) Which word did it come from? (\textbf{\ur{ہوئی}}, \emph{huī}, \textquotedblleft{}happened (in pleased to meet you)\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
